# Locality, light cones, and propagation {#sec-locality}

## Why a nonrelativistic lattice has a speed

The Schrödinger equation contains no explicit speed limit. Nevertheless a
finite-range spin Hamiltonian cannot transmit a substantial local perturbation
arbitrarily far in a fixed time. The reason is constructive: a nested sequence
of local interactions must connect the perturbation to the detector. This
chapter develops that argument and distinguishes several velocities often
called a light-cone speed.

We assume finite-dimensional sites on a bounded-degree lattice, bounded local
interactions, and a finite interaction range. These hypotheses are part of the
result. Power-law interactions and unbounded bosons require modified bounds,
discussed in [chapter 29](29-long-range-gauge.qmd).

## A commutator as a signal detector

Prepare a state $\rho$ and optionally apply a weak local kick
$V_A=e^{-i\epsilon A}$ before evolving. A later measurement of $B$ changes by

$$
\delta\langle B(t)\rangle
=i\epsilon\operatorname{Tr}(\rho[A,B(t)])+O(\epsilon^2).
$$ {#eq-locality-signal}

Therefore the operator norm $\|[A,B(t)]\|$ bounds the signal in every initial
state. The norm is the largest singular value. A small expectation of a
commutator in one state is a weaker statement; cancellation can hide a large
operator. Squared commutators averaged in a thermal state instead lead to
out-of-time-order correlators and butterfly fronts.

For initially disjoint supports the equal-time commutator vanishes exactly.
At later times it is usually nonzero but exponentially small outside a cone.
Thus the lattice cone is approximate, with tails, rather than a strict
relativistic causal boundary.

## The path argument

Take $H=\sum_{\langle xy\rangle}h_{xy}$ with
$\|h_{xy}\|\leq J$ and a maximum lattice coordination number $z$. In the
series
$A(t)=\sum_{n\geq0}(it)^n\operatorname{ad}_H^n(A)/n!$,
a nonzero contribution to $[A(t),B]$ must contain a connected chain of
interactions from the support of $A$ to that of $B$. A range-one term can
advance the chain by at most one bond. At graph distance $r$, at least $r$
such steps are required.

Naively counting every expanding support can overestimate the series badly.
The useful proof first writes a differential inequality for the commutator
norm, factors out terms acting solely within the current support by unitary
conjugation, and iterates only interactions crossing its boundary. For
single-site endpoints the resulting connected-walk bound has the schematic
form, with a harmless geometry-dependent prefactor $C$,

$$
\|[A_x(t),B_y]\|
\leq C\|A_x\|\|B_y\|
\sum_{n\geq r}\frac{(2J|t|)^n}{n!}\,N_n(x,y),
\qquad N_n(x,y)\leq c_z^n.
$$ {#eq-locality-walkbound}

Here $c_z$ is a bounded geometry constant controlled by coordination and
interaction overlap. Its precise value depends on the path convention. The
exact constants depend on the interaction decomposition;
the essential content is a factorial in order and an exponential number of
paths. For any $\mu>0$, $1_{n\geq r}\leq e^{\mu(n-r)}$, giving

$$
\|[A_x(t),B_y]\|
\leq C\|A_x\|\|B_y\|
e^{-\mu r+2Jc_ze^\mu|t|}
=C\|A_x\|\|B_y\|e^{-\mu(r-v_\mu|t|)},
\quad v_\mu=\frac{2Jc_ze^\mu}{\mu}.
$$ {#eq-locality-lr}

For finite support regions there are additional support-size factors. This
Lieb–Robinson form is a rigorous type of bound under the stated local
hypotheses, although the displayed elementary constants are deliberately loose.
Its speed $v_\mu$ is an upper bound, not a prediction of a measured front.
Modern proofs optimize the geometry and decay assumptions
[@bravyi2006locality].

## From a commutator bound to a local approximation

Let $A(t)$ be approximated by evolving only inside a ball of radius $R$ around
its initial support. A Duhamel expansion compares the two evolutions. Their
difference is an integral of commutators with omitted boundary terms. Applying
the bound gives an error of the form
$\|A(t)-A_R(t)\|\lesssim\mathrm{poly}(R)e^{-\mu(R-v|t|)}$.
For a fixed local observable, one can therefore simulate a sufficiently large
causal neighborhood instead of the entire thermodynamic system. This does not
make arbitrarily long times cheap: the required neighborhood grows with time,
and its Hilbert-space dimension grows exponentially with its volume.

The same argument bounds the rate at which initially independent regions can
develop correlations. A local observable in $X$ and one in $Y$ can each spread
toward an intermediate region. This is why a correlation cone after a global
quench can involve a separation speed of order twice a quasiparticle speed.
An initially entangled state may already have long-distance correlations; local
evolution does not need to create them. Assumptions about initial correlations
are indispensable in a correlation-growth statement.

## A propagation front you can calculate exactly

For the free chain
$H=(J/2)\sum_j(c_j^\dagger c_{j+1}+\mathrm{h.c.})$, start with one particle
at the origin. Its amplitude at site $r$ is

$$
\psi_r(t)=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{dk}{2\pi}
e^{ikr-iJt\cos k}=(-i)^r\mathcal J_r(Jt).
$$ {#eq-locality-freefront}

Stationary phase requires $r/t=-J\sin k$. There are real stationary points
only when $|r/t|\leq|J|$. Outside this region the Fourier phases cannot remain
aligned, leaving rapidly suppressed tails. The maximum group velocity $|J|$
is the actual ballistic edge of this single-particle problem. It is much smaller
than the loose bound above.

Near a maximum-velocity point, the second derivative of the phase vanishes and
the leading nontrivial term is cubic. Writing $r=Jt+\delta r$, the phase has
the structure $q\delta r+O(Jt q^3)$. Balancing the terms gives
$q\sim t^{-1/3}$ and $\delta r\sim t^{1/3}$. The edge therefore has an
Airy-type dispersive width. A noisy chaotic circuit's operator front commonly
broadens as $t^{1/2}$ instead. Ballistic position does not determine front
broadening, and a free-particle front is not a demonstration of scrambling.

## Several velocities, several questions

| Quantity | Definition | What it can tell you |
|---|---|---|
| Lieb–Robinson velocity | A speed appearing in a state-independent norm bound | An upper limit on substantial local signaling under its hypotheses |
| Maximum group velocity | $\max_k|\partial_k\epsilon(k)|$ for specified quasiparticles | A propagating excitation edge when that quasiparticle description applies |
| Butterfly velocity | Motion of a specified OTOC/operator-growth contour | The spread of operator influence in a stated ensemble |
| Entanglement velocity | Entropy production rate divided by equilibrium entropy density, with geometry specified | Growth across a cut in a stated quench regime |
| Hydrodynamic spreading scale | Width such as $\sqrt{Dt}$ | Motion of conserved density, which can be slower than information |

There are inequalities among some velocities under suitable assumptions. There
is no general rule setting all of them equal. A conserved density can diffuse
while a nonconserved operator spreads ballistically in the same system. An
experiment measuring a density correlation probes neither the operator norm
nor automatically the entanglement production rate.

## Entanglement production and computational cost

Only Hamiltonian terms crossing a spatial cut can immediately change the
entanglement across it; terms confined to either side are local unitaries and
leave the Schmidt values invariant. Bounded interactions and finite local
dimension therefore constrain the entropy production rate by a constant times
the number of terms crossing the cut, with a logarithmic local-dimension factor.
The boundary-area structure is robust, while the constant is model dependent
[@bravyi2006locality]. Starting from a product state, entropy can grow at most
linearly in time across a fixed one-dimensional cut.

This statement is an upper bound. An integrable system, disorder, kinetic
constraints, or weak interactions can produce much slower growth. If
$S\sim s v_E t$ in an ergodic quench, an MPS representing the state with small
error generally needs a bond dimension growing exponentially in time. Locality
helps identify the relevant space, but does not remove the entanglement barrier.

## Research bridges and limits

The cold-atom light-cone experiment [@cheneau2012lightcone] measured parity
correlations after a quench and interpreted their propagation using pairs of
quasiparticles. A first reproduction is a free-particle or strong-coupling
pair model, followed by a comparison with interacting simulation. The limitation
of the simple model is its treatment of collisions and finite-density effects.

For long-range interactions, the relevant norm and task become decisive.
Tran and collaborators derived a hierarchy of cones for different notions of
information propagation [@tran2020hierarchy]. Their result motivates asking
which error norm an algorithm controls and which observable an experiment
measures. An apparent violation of a short-range cone is not a violation of
causality when the Hamiltonian lies outside its hypotheses.

## Exercises and worked solutions

1. Starting from a local kick, derive the signal formula and its norm bound.
   Does a vanishing expectation of the commutator for one initial state prove
   the absence of signaling for all states?
2. Optimize $v_\mu=2Jc_ze^\mu/\mu$ for $\mu>0$. Compare with the XX
   maximum group velocity and explain why the result need not be sharp.
3. Derive the $t^{1/3}$ free-front width by retaining the first nonvanishing
   derivatives at $k=\pi/2$. What additional assumptions would be needed to
   infer a noisy-front diffusion constant?
4. Prepare two far-separated Bell pairs and evolve with a local Hamiltonian.
   Explain why an initially nonzero connected correlation outside a cone does
   not contradict a bound on newly generated correlations.
5. Numerically evolve a single-particle tight-binding chain and compare
   thresholds of $|\psi_r|^2$ at different small values. Determine how a
   threshold-dependent speed approaches the group-velocity edge.

**Solution to 1.** Expand
$V_A^\dagger B(t)V_A=B(t)+i\epsilon[A,B(t)]+O(\epsilon^2)$ and take the
trace. Since $|\operatorname{Tr}\rho C|\leq\|C\|$, the stated bound
follows. A special state can have zero expectation even for a nonzero operator,
so absence of one response is not the uniform statement.

**Solution to 2.** Differentiating $e^\mu/\mu$ gives
$e^\mu(\mu-1)/\mu^2$, so the minimum is at $\mu=1$ and the bound is
$2eJc_z$. It counts all walks and ignores destructive quantum interference and
the detailed dispersion. A rigorous speed can be substantially larger than an
actual front without being false.
